To euthanize something (or someone) means to deliberately and painlessly end its life, usually to prevent it from suffering. It is an act done out of mercy, not malice.

Think of it this way: if a living being is in severe pain with no hope of recovery, and continuing to live would only mean more suffering, the decision might be made to end that life quickly and without pain. That act — the deliberate, compassionate ending of a life to spare it suffering — is what "to euthanize" means.

Where you'll most commonly see this word: In everyday language, "euthanize" is used most often in a veterinary (animal care) context. When a pet is old, terminally ill, or severely injured, a veterinarian may euthanize the animal. The owner and doctor agree that the animal's quality of life has fallen so low that a peaceful, immediate death is kinder than letting it suffer through its remaining days. This is sometimes called "putting an animal to sleep" or "putting an animal down" — those are gentler, informal ways of saying the same thing.

When used for humans, the word "euthanize" carries much heavier legal and ethical weight, and you'll often hear the related noun "euthanasia" instead. Human euthanasia is legal in only a small number of countries and regions around the world.

How is it done? The most common method is a lethal injection — a drug (or combination of drugs) that first makes the being unconscious and then stops the heart. The process is designed to be painless and rapid. Because it is medically controlled, it is very different from simply "killing" something.

Who performs it? A licensed professional almost always carries it out. For animals, that's a veterinarian. For humans (where it is legal), it is a physician. This professional requirement is important — it separates euthanasia from other forms of killing. It is a clinical, controlled act governed by rules, ethics, and law.

The intent is everything. What makes "euthanize" a distinct word is the motivation behind the act. The intent is never to punish, harm, or destroy — it is always to relieve suffering. This is why it is called a "mercy killing" in plain English. The word mercy here is key: you are doing something painful (ending a life) for a compassionate reason (ending suffering).

Voluntary vs. involuntary euthanasia (for humans): When it comes to people, an important distinction exists:

  • Voluntary euthanasia is when the person themselves requests to have their life ended because they are suffering and do not wish to continue living. They are making an informed, conscious choice.
  • Involuntary euthanasia is when the decision is made by others — for example, when a patient is unconscious or unable to communicate — based on what is believed to be in that person's best interest.

This distinction matters a great deal in ethics and law. It is one reason why euthanasia for humans is one of the most debated topics in medicine and philosophy.

Active vs. passive euthanasia: You may also encounter these terms:

  • Active euthanasia means taking a direct action to end a life — like giving a lethal injection.
  • Passive euthanasia means withdrawing life-sustaining treatment (such as removing a ventilator or stopping medication) and allowing the person or animal to die naturally from their illness.

Both fall under the broader concept of euthanasia, but active euthanasia is generally more controversial.
How it differs from similar concepts:

• Killing is a neutral or negative word that simply means ending a life. It carries no information about why or how. Euthanizing is a specific kind of killing — merciful, intentional, and professionally controlled.
  • Murder is the unlawful and malicious killing of a person. Euthanasia, when legal and properly carried out, is the opposite in spirit.
  • Assisted suicide (or "physician-assisted dying") is slightly different: here, the doctor provides the means (such as a prescription for a lethal drug), but the patient themselves takes the final action to end their own life. In euthanasia, the professional administers it directly.

The emotional weight of the word: "Euthanize" is not an emotionally neutral word. Even when the act is considered the right and compassionate choice, it carries grief, moral seriousness, and weight. People who euthanize a beloved pet, for example, often describe it as one of the hardest decisions of their lives, even knowing it was the kindest one. The word acknowledges that ending a life — regardless of the reason — is never trivial.

• "The dog had cancer in its final stage, and the vet advised the family to euthanize him to spare him further pain."
  • "The legislature is debating whether to allow doctors to euthanize terminally ill patients who request it."
  • "After the horse broke its leg in a way that could not be healed, the difficult decision was made to euthanize it."

• Euthanasia (noun) — the act or practice of euthanizing. "The family chose euthanasia for their suffering cat."
  • Euthanized (past tense) — "The animal was euthanized yesterday."
  • Euthanizing (present participle) — "The doctor is not in favor of euthanizing patients without their consent."

In summary: To euthanize is to deliberately and painlessly end a life — most commonly an animal's — in order to relieve unbearable suffering, when there is no hope of meaningful recovery. It is always done with the intention of mercy, typically by a licensed professional, and it is one of the most morally complex acts in medicine because it sits at the intersection of compassion, law, ethics, and the profound value of life.
